newsitem.title: USA: "Animal Doctor" is just what the vet ordered.
newsitem.headline: "Animal Doctor" is just what the vet ordered.

text.p: "I Can Be An Animal Doctor" is a doggone good CD-ROM game for youngsters whose love of animals makes them want to be a veterinarian.

Designed for children ages 6 to 10 (but older kids will like it as well), "Animal Doctor" lets them visit four habitats of an animal park in search of sick or injured animals, bring the creatures into a field hospital and run some pseudo-tests to find out what's wrong.

By dragging a stethoscope to a creature, for example, the child is told whether the heart rate is normal. A magnifying glass gives a closeup look at the eyes, snout, legs or fur. Clicking on a microscope produces an image of a blood or skin sample, which the child has to put into focus by sliding a bar; if something odd is found (and a normal sample appears on the left for comparison), the would-be vet has to highlight it.
Guiding the youngster through the steps is a cartoon veterinarian, Dr. Max Rigby, who points out the abnormalities and ultimately comes up with a diagnosis.

Then Dr. Rigby lets players select one of three possible treatments. In the case of a bear that has been stung by bees, the child must use tweezers, give antihistamines and dab on a topical solution to reduce the swelling. (I assume the game was joking with me when I treated an elephant for a sprained knee and the doctor advised that "the elephant should stay in bed for two weeks.")
After each successful treatment, the child gets a "Thank You" card from the animal.

And there's a lot more to "Animal Doctor" than playing veterinarian. There are brief biographical sketches on famous vets, a quick description of how students should prepare to become a veterinarian and a section on caring for different kinds of pets, from dogs and cats to hermit crabs and pot belly pigs.
There are also six games.

"Weigh Cool," which is essentially a math game, lets players stack pianos, cars, kids, soda machines and other objects onto a scale in an attempt to match the weight of an animal. "Desert Treasures" teaches about camouflage by challenging kids to find animals hidden in the landscape. "Feeding Frenzy" (which takes place in a cartoon restaurant) makes players pick the right food for the right animal. If you try to serve tacos to a cat, the cat vomits and sends the plate crashing to the floor.

The only problems I uncovered were minor. It would be nice if the game explained why an animal with a sprained ankle might also have a faster heart rate or weigh less than normal. Also, some of the instructions become repetitious, and there's no easy way to bypass them.
But the flaws are minor. Kids who love animals will find that this CD-ROM from Cloud 9 Interactive (Windows/Macintosh, $30, http://www.cloud9int.com) is just what the doctor -- or the vet -- ordered.

"InventorLabs: Transportation" (Windows/Macintosh, $30, 800-829-7962, http://www.hminet.com) celebrates the discovery of the first working airplane, automobile and locomotive by letting you meet actors portraying the inventors and by recreating the laboratories that gave birth to those breakthroughs.
It's a shame this CD-ROM doesn't show the same quality workmanship and attention to detail as the inventors themselves.

This second instalment in HMI's "InventorLabs" series has several things going for it. While you're inside the labs you can use Quicktime virtual reality to change your view of the scene and examine some of the devices used to build or fine-tune each invention.

Visit the Wright Cycle Company in Dayton, Ohio, for example, and Wilbur and Orville Wright let you put miniature wings in their wind tunnel to see which one gives the best lift. You can also test propellers to see which provides the most power.
Then you can travel to the sand dunes of Kitty Hawk to choose a rudder and seat position and see what effect they have on the craft.
But this educational game can't get the basic details right.

If I positioned the airplane's seat too far back and ran a simulated flight, the text correctly told me, "The plane tilted back suddenly. Perhaps the problem is that there is too much weight in the back."
Unfortunately, the game ran the wrong video. Instead of showing the plane tilting up too far, it ploughed into the ground.

To compound the error, the game played the wrong narration. Wilbur Wright told me, "The airplane did not climb high enough. Perhaps there is too much weight in the front." (Remember, I put the seat too far back.)

"InventorLabs: Transportation" can't even give basic instructions correctly. The opening demonstration told me to use the shift key to zoom back and the control key to zoom in. In reality, the reverse was true.

And in the portion of the game that lets you build your own vehicle to race across various terrains, the clock on the timed trials was off. A race that took 53 seconds according to my watch ended up being logged as taking 27.5 seconds.
Houghton Mifflin Interactive should recall this game for retooling.
(Gene Emery is a columnist who covers science and technology. His Internet address is gene.emery(at)prodigy.com. Any opinions in the column are his alone.)
